title: One in Four European Pilots Fly When Tired
paragraphs: When we get on a plane, we expect the pilots to be well rested. However, a new survey suggests that many pilots in Europe are flying when they are too tired.

The survey was published in October 2026 by the European Cockpit Association, or ECA, which represents pilots in Europe. The report was written by Baines Simmons, an aviation safety company. Between August 4 and September 7, 2026, about 7,200 airline pilots in 32 European countries answered questions about tiredness at work.

The results were worrying. When pilots felt too tired to fly safely, only 37.2% said that they reported it. Almost one in four pilots, or 24.2%, said that they usually did not report it and flew anyway.

In addition, 76.8% of the pilots said they had experienced at least one "microsleep" while flying a plane in the previous four weeks. A microsleep is when a person falls asleep for a very short time, often without knowing it. Furthermore, 38.8% said they usually or always did not get enough rest between work periods.

Why don't more pilots report being tired? According to the survey, many pilots are afraid of what might happen if they do. For example, 69.1% said they were worried about negative results if they refused to work longer hours. Only 11.9% said they trusted their airline's system for reporting tiredness.
The survey also found that the situation had not improved since the ECA's last survey in 2023.

The ECA wants stronger protection for pilots who report being tired. It also wants airlines to manage tiredness better, and it wants governments and European aviation authorities to check airlines more carefully.
However, it is important to note that pilots chose to take part in the survey, so the results may not represent all pilots in Europe.
